rules.name: Reconnaissance
rules.statement: Read the relevant code, configuration, instructions, and repository state before proposing or changing behavior. Match the repository's established patterns unless its source of truth requires a correction.
rules.rationale: Accurate changes depend on repository context.

rules.name: Scope
rules.statement: Keep work inside the user's requested outcome. Read-only discovery may expand enough to establish truth; external writes and materially different changes require explicit authority.
rules.rationale: Scope control protects user intent and external systems.

rules.name: Evidence
rules.statement: Run the command that proves each claimed result and report complete, blocked, drifted, and not-installed states separately. A partial or inconclusive check is not a pass.
rules.rationale: Delivery claims need reproducible evidence.

rules.name: Propose first
rules.statement: Before building a new feature or visual direction, record the problem, options with evidence (a mock or prototype for UI), and the choice in the repository's decision log; fixing drift from an existing rule needs no proposal.
rules.rationale: A written problem, options, and evidence let the owner choose a direction before it is built, while conformance fixes stay fast.

enforcement.check: Decision-log review before a new feature or visual direction

rules.name: Isolation
rules.statement: Implement feature work on a feature branch in an isolated worktree when the current checkout contains unrelated work or the task spans repositories.
rules.rationale: Isolation prevents cross-task contamination.

rules.name: Preservation
rules.statement: Preserve unrelated dirty changes. Never reset, discard, or force-push the default branch. Resolve exact targets before destructive actions and prefer recoverable operations.
rules.rationale: User work must remain recoverable.

rules.name: Secret safety
rules.statement: Keep credential values out of source, prompts, logs, fixtures, generated artifacts, and terminal output. Store only references or documented environment-variable names.
rules.rationale: Secrets exposed in code or logs are difficult to revoke.

rules.name: Boundaries
rules.statement: Validate untrusted input at the system boundary, parameterize database queries, redact sensitive data, and expose stable public errors instead of internal details.
rules.rationale: Boundary controls prevent injection and data disclosure.

rules.name: Behavior tests
rules.statement: New or changed business behavior requires a test that exercises the real boundary and covers the relevant success, edge, and failure paths.
rules.rationale: Boundary tests protect intended behavior.

rules.name: Repository gate
rules.statement: Before commit or review, run the repository's documented CI-equivalent checks. At minimum, compile or build changed production code when no stronger command exists.
rules.rationale: The repository gate catches integration errors before review.

rules.name: Resource budgets
rules.statement: Keep shipped surfaces inside recorded budgets and measure a change that could cross one: web pages LCP ≤ 2.5 s and INP ≤ 200 ms at p75, API endpoints p95 ≤ 300 ms, apps cold launch ≤ 1 s with no idle CPU wake-ups, and bundle or image size growth over 5 % per release explained in the pull request.
rules.rationale: Performance regressions ship silently unless each surface has a number to stay under and changes near it are measured.

enforcement.check: Budget review with a recorded measurement

rules.name: Normative vocabulary
rules.statement: Use uppercase BCP 14 requirement words only when a rule has normative force; do not create additional machine-enforced requirement levels.
rules.rationale: A closed vocabulary makes rule severity interpretable and auditable.

rules.name: Stable rule identifiers
rules.statement: Treat rule IDs as immutable opaque identifiers; never reuse an ID after renaming, deprecation, retirement, splitting, or merging.
rules.rationale: Stable IDs preserve audit, suppression, and historical evidence links.

rules.name: Time-bounded exceptions
rules.statement: Record every exception with its owner, reason, exact scope, approval, and expiry or review date before relying on it.
rules.rationale: Exceptions need accountability and a planned review point.

rules.name: Real checks
rules.statement: Name the file behind every blocking `ci`, `lint`, or `test` enforcement of a project rule in its `path`; the project checker fails when that file is missing, unless a `pending` date no more than 14 days old marks a check still being built.
rules.rationale: A rule that cites a missing check reads as enforced while nothing runs; resolving each named check to a file makes that claim verifiable.

rules.name: Portable repository names
rules.statement: Use lowercase ASCII kebab-case for repository directories, documentation, and assets by default; preserve ecosystem-native source filenames and record an explicit repository exception when a tool requires another form.
rules.rationale: Portable names reduce cross-platform ambiguity without overriding ecosystem requirements.

rules.name: Delivery names
rules.statement: Use `codex/<short-kebab-topic>` branches by default, Conventional Commit subjects in imperative English, and imperative English pull-request titles.
rules.rationale: Consistent delivery names make history and automation predictable.

rules.name: Release identifiers
rules.statement: Use SemVer `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` release tags and never move a published release tag or change a historical identifier.
rules.rationale: Immutable identifiers keep releases traceable.

rules.name: Environment variable names
rules.statement: Use upper snake case environment variables with a product or domain prefix, and never put secret values in tracked configuration.
rules.rationale: Portable variable names and secret separation prevent configuration leaks.

rules.name: Native code identifiers
rules.statement: Follow the language and framework formatter or linter already authoritative in the repository for code identifiers.
rules.rationale: Cross-language rules should not supersede authoritative ecosystem tooling.

rules.name: Scoped delivery names
rules.statement: Use `<type>(<scope>)/<short-kebab-topic>` branches by default, where `<type>` is a Conventional Commits type (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `ci`, `build`, `revert`, or `style`) and `<scope>` is a short kebab-case area as in `feat(app)/device-auth` or `fix(api)/rate-limit`; keep Conventional Commit subjects in imperative English and imperative English pull-request titles.
rules.rationale: Scoped branch names keep history and automation predictable while recording the change type and area.

rules.name: Evidence-backed findings
rules.statement: Report only evidence-backed P0 or P1 findings with tight file and line references and the applicable stable rule ID when one exists; suppress style-only or speculative comments.
rules.rationale: High-signal review comments improve actionable feedback.

rules.name: Automated releases
rules.statement: Cut every actively developed repository's releases through the fleet release bot: the reusable `Misoto22/ci` release workflow running release-please in manifest mode as the `misoto22-release-bot` GitHub App. Derive the version, `CHANGELOG.md`, and GitHub Release from Conventional Commits; never hand-edit a version field and never move a tag. Configure a multi-package npm workspace with the `node-workspace` plugin and linked versions so the repository still tags one `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.
rules.rationale: One automated release path keeps versions, changelogs, and tags derived from the same reviewed history instead of from hand edits.

rules.name: Changelog vocabulary
rules.statement: List only `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `revert`, `docs`, and `refactor` in `changelog-sections`. Never list `chore`, `ci`, `build`, `test`, or `style`, not even hidden, because release-please then considers those commits for a bump and cuts a patch release for a lone housekeeping commit.
rules.rationale: A housekeeping type listed in the changelog sections becomes a release trigger.

rules.name: Verified releases
rules.statement: After a release, confirm the tag, the published artifact, and the result people receive (live version, store or TestFlight build, package index) before calling it done; a green workflow alone is not evidence.
rules.rationale: Release automation can exit green without a tag, an upload, or a deploy, so only the delivered result proves a release.

enforcement.check: Post-release verification recorded in the release report

rules.name: Linux pull-request gate
rules.statement: Run pull-request checks on Linux runners, declare a `concurrency` group keyed on the ref with `cancel-in-progress` for pull requests, and apply path filters wherever a change cannot alter a check's result.
rules.rationale: Linux is the cheapest hosted tier, and superseding stale runs stops a pull-request gate from spending the account's quota on results nobody reads.

rules.name: macOS off the pull-request path
rules.statement: Run GitHub-hosted macOS only for tag pushes, scheduled runs, or path-gated platform changes; gate an Apple-platform pull request on a self-hosted runner or a Linux SwiftPM package test instead.
rules.rationale: Hosted macOS minutes bill at ten times the Linux rate, so a macOS leg on every pull request is the largest avoidable cost in the fleet.

rules.name: Pinned actions
rules.statement: Reference every third-party action and reusable workflow by full commit SHA with a trailing version comment, and keep those references current through Dependabot's `github-actions` ecosystem.
rules.rationale: A mutable tag lets an upstream repository change what runs inside a release-capable job; a pinned SHA plus an update bot keeps the supply chain both fixed and current.

rules.name: Required checks by name
rules.statement: Require the repository's own CI job or jobs and `pr-title / pr-title` in the branch ruleset, and write a reusable-workflow job's check context as `<caller job id> / <called job name>`.
rules.rationale: A required check is matched by its rendered context string, so a bare job name protects nothing while appearing to.

rules.name: Native toolchain
rules.statement: Use the repository's pinned Python manager and commands. When the repository uses `uv`, keep its lock file authoritative; use pytest for tests and Ruff for configured lint/format gates.
rules.rationale: Pinned toolchains make Python results reproducible.

rules.name: PEP 8 names
rules.statement: Follow PEP 8 naming: `snake_case` modules, functions, methods, and variables; `CapWords` classes, with an `Error` suffix for exceptions; `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` module-level constants; and a single leading underscore for non-public names.
rules.rationale: PEP 8 is the shared vocabulary of Python readers and tooling.

rules.name: Python intent names
rules.statement: Name functions that act with verb phrases (`load_config`, `send_digest`), name Booleans as predicates with `is_`, `has_`, `can_`, or `should_`, and use single-letter names only for loop indices and comprehension variables.
rules.rationale: Intent-revealing names make control flow readable without tracing values.

rules.name: Repository contract
rules.statement: Follow the checked-in package manager, workspace boundaries, compiler settings, lint rules, and test runner. Prefer existing types and components over parallel local abstractions; verify typecheck and the affected test/build path.
rules.rationale: Project tooling and shared abstractions define the TypeScript contract.

enforcement.check: Typecheck and affected test or build

rules.name: TypeScript identifier case
rules.statement: Use `camelCase` for variables, functions, and methods, `PascalCase` for classes, types, interfaces, enums, and React components, and `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` only for true constants such as fixed configuration values; do not prefix interfaces with `I`.
rules.rationale: One casing scheme per identifier kind lets readers tell values, types, and components apart at a glance.

rules.name: TypeScript intent names
rules.statement: Name functions with verb phrases (`fetchInvoices`, `formatDate`) and Booleans as predicates with `is`, `has`, `can`, or `should` (`isLoading`, `hasAccess`).
rules.rationale: Intent-revealing names make component and hook logic readable without tracing values.

rules.name: TypeScript file names
rules.statement: Follow the framework's file conventions, such as Next.js App Router reserved files (`page.tsx`, `layout.tsx`, `route.ts`), kebab-case route segments, `[param]` dynamic segments, and `(group)` route groups; elsewhere keep the file casing the repository already uses.
rules.rationale: Framework routers derive behavior from file names, so those names are part of the contract.

rules.name: Executable truth
rules.statement: Keep commands, paths, version claims, architecture diagrams, and public examples aligned with the current implementation. Verify links and generated documentation before review.
rules.rationale: Documentation is a user-facing implementation surface.

rules.name: One owner per fact
rules.statement: Give every product fact (URL, identifier, limit, version, user-facing string, style value) one owning module or repository; everything else imports it, generates it, or vendors it with recorded provenance, and a copy that cannot be generated has a check that fails when it differs.
rules.rationale: The same fact written in two places drifts; one owner plus generation or a comparison check keeps every copy true.

enforcement.check: Single-owner review of new constants, strings, and style values

rules.name: Cohesive files
rules.statement: Keep one concept per file. A production source file over 400 lines may not grow: `.rulesync/file-size-baseline.json` records the ones that already are, and its counts only fall.
rules.rationale: Large files mix concepts and grow by default; a lower-only baseline stops the growth without blocking work on existing files.

rules.name: Latest stable
rules.statement: Adopt and keep the newest stable release of every dependency, tool, runtime, base image, and action, never a pre-release or a scaffold default; hold one back only with a README note naming the blocker and a review date.
rules.rationale: Old versions accumulate security fixes and migration cost; a written blocker keeps every held-back version deliberate.

enforcement.check: Dependency review against the README exceptions

rules.name: Tracked versions
rules.statement: Give every lock file, `Package.swift`, and `Dockerfile` a Dependabot entry for its ecosystem and directory, and declare each runtime once, in `.python-version` or `.node-version`, so every other pin agrees with it.
rules.rationale: A lock file without an updater and a runtime pinned in several places drift unnoticed; one declaration and full updater coverage keep them current.
